title: Charging Dicke and Tavis--Cummings quantum batteries with a $\mathcal{PT}$-symmetric lossy--gain cavity pair
authors: Shiqing Tang, Qing Yu, Ying Li, Cuilu Zhai, Zhao-Hui Peng, Wangjun Lu
abstract: We study how a parity--time-symmetric photonic environment changes the charging of Dicke and Tavis--Cummings quantum batteries. For atoms prepared in the collective ground state the excitation number grows as the square of the charging time, with a coefficient set by the initial mean photon number; the counter-rotating terms of the Dicke model add one to four times that number. Conservation of the total excitation number turns this into an exact ceiling on the stored Tavis--Cummings energy, the transition energy times the smaller of the photon and atom numbers, met numerically to within two per cent, which the Dicke terms overshoot by a few per cent at ultrastrong coupling. We then couple a battery to a lossy--gain pair, keeping the parity--time symmetry intact by putting an identical battery in each cavity; the closed moment system puts the exceptional point at the loss rate. Below it the gain cavity fills and the gain-side battery charges while the lossy-side one stays empty; above it photons are shuttled away and dissipated. Solving the full Lindblad equation with batched Monte--Carlo wave functions, we find that the gain-side battery gains thirty-nine, twenty-six and twenty-eight per cent in stored energy, power and ergotropy in the broken phase and loses sixty-five, thirty-five and sixty-five per cent deep in the unbroken phase, where the lossy-side battery overtakes it. Restoring the counter-rotating terms leaves all of this unchanged within the statistical error; what they add is a reactive oscillation at twice the transition frequency that does no net work but nearly doubles the peak of the instantaneous power. The extra energy is of lower quality, the recoverable fraction dropping from about ninety-eight to ninety per cent. The optimum sits on the broken side, close to but not at the exceptional point.
summary: This paper analyzes how coupling quantum batteries, modeled by Dicke and Tavis-Cummings Hamiltonians, to a $\mathcal{PT}$-symmetric lossy-gain cavity pair affects energy charging. Using advanced numerical techniques, the authors map out distinct charging regimes around the exceptional point, finding that the optimal energy extraction occurs in the broken phase. The results highlight the strong control offered by engineered non-Hermitian environments over quantum energy storage.
main_problem: The study investigates how coupling a quantum battery (Dicke or Tavis-Cummings model) to a parity-time ($\mathcal{PT}$)-symmetric lossy-gain photonic environment alters its charging dynamics.
main_result: The charging dynamics are highly dependent on the spectral regime relative to the exceptional point (EP); the optimal charging point is found in the broken phase, and the counter-rotating terms introduce a reactive oscillation without net work.
method: The dynamics are solved by numerically solving the full Lindblad equation using batched Monte-Carlo wave functions, alongside analytical derivations for short-time scaling laws.
model_or_system: The system comprises quantum batteries (Dicke and Tavis-Cummings) coupled to a $\mathcal{PT}$-symmetric cavity pair, which acts as the environment. The dynamics are governed by the Lindblad master equation.
key_observables: Stored energy, power, and ergotropy gained/lost in the gain-side versus lossy-side battery; excitation number growth; and the location of the exceptional point.
important_parameters: The loss rate ($\gamma$), the coupling strength ($J$), and the proximity to the exceptional point (EP) are critical parameters defining the system's behavior.
main_assumptions: The analysis assumes the batteries are identical to maintain $\mathcal{PT}$ symmetry, and the Tavis-Cummings treatment is deemed sufficient despite the presence of Dicke terms.
figures_summary: The notes reference figures showing short-time scaling of excitation number, energy bounds for TC and Dicke models, and the dependence of observables on the loss rate relative to the EP.
paper_structure: The paper is structured by first analyzing isolated batteries (Dicke/TC) charged by a reservoir, then analyzing the cavity pair dynamics to find the EP, and finally coupling the battery to the pair to study charging in both the broken and unbroken phases.
why_interesting: This work directly addresses open quantum systems, cavity QED, and quantum energy storage, providing quantitative insights into how engineered non-Hermitian environments can control energy transfer and extraction efficiency in quantum devices.
